extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, inventors, judges, and students of patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for writing and construing patent specifications and claims — what a specification must disclose, how claims may be framed, and how courts/juries evaluate sufficiency, ambiguity, and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to claim multiple modes/substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor 'may claim as many modes as he pleases, provided always that the claim is limited to such as he has invented, and as are substantially new.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee is not limited to a single mode or a single set of ingredients; he may extend his claim to substitutes of the same general character to prevent easy evasion. Example: a patent for a compound naming phosphorus, chalk, and glue may also claim gums or other glutinous substances of the same general character. Risk: if any of the combinations (original or substituted) were known before, the patent may be avoided as to those combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming variations without minute directions is acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficient for the patentee to state the modes which he contemplates as best, and his claim will not be void, as too vague or comprehensive, although he claims the variations from those modes as being equally his invention, without describing the manner of producing those variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For machines, the statute requires specification of the principal and the several modes contemplated, but the patentee need not enter into minute description of every possible formal variation; indicating which variations he claims beyond his preferred modes suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between claim construction (law) and enablement (fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification discloses what the invention is is a question for the court (construction of the patent); whether it sufficiently describes the mode of carrying the invention into practice (enablement) is a question for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts construe the scope and meaning of the claim as a matter of law; juries (or fact-finders) decide whether a skilled mechanic could make the thing from the directions given. Example: description of rib thickness in a cotton-gin: sufficiency to make a proper rib is a factual question for those skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity that cannot be elucidated invalidates patent irrespective of motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Where ambiguity exists in the specification to such a degree that it cannot be elucidated, it is immaterial whether it had its origin in the mala fides of the patentee, or in haste or incompetency; ambiguity or claiming too much is the vital test of validity, not motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts focus on the sufficiency and clarity of the specification itself; intent or explanations about why ambiguity arose do not save an otherwise unclear claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-fullness (introducing useless/unnecessary matter) can vitiate the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If things wholly useless and unnecessary are introduced into the specification, as if they were essential, although terms are intelligible and necessary description present, the patent may be declared void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English authorities presume such useless insertions were intended to overload and cloud the description to mislead the public and conceal the real invention. Examples: listing ingredients not needed to make the claimed article may void the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose the best mode and advantageous circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee is bound to disclose the most advantageous mode known to him, and any circumstance conducive to the advantageous operation of his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose the best mode (or later improvements made before filing) can subject the patentee to the burden of proving the improvement was made after issuing the patent; otherwise, courts may presume the patentee withheld the best method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improved mode discovered after patent issues: patentee bears burden to prove timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Where it seems the patentee has an improved mode of working his machine different from the specification, he must show that he made the improvement subsequently to the issuing of his patent, otherwise it will be presumed he did not disclose the best method known to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patentee cannot show the improvement was post-issue, courts may treat the specification as having omitted the best known method and may penalize the patentee accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable practising the invention for infringement to exist
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringement will not have taken place unless the invention can be practised completely by following the specification; if the patent does not fully describe anything essential to making or doing the thing patented, there will be no infringement by others' fresh invention of omitted processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement requires a copy made after and agreeing with the principle laid down in the patent. If essential steps or parts are withheld, third parties who actually make the invention may not infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to describe each substantially different modification made
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of an inventor to describe in his specification each substantially different modification of his invention which he has made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inventor has multiple distinct versions, he must disclose them; failure to describe a materially different prior modification may be problematic (e.g., reissue disputes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of terms rendering the specification unintelligible is fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity produced by misuse of terms so as to render the specification unintelligible will be as fatal as any other defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use of a generic or nonexistent trade term ('fossil-salt' when only 'sal-gem' is usable) or calling for 'finest and purest chemical white-lead' when no such term exists in the trade makes the specification defective. Minor typographical word mistakes are immaterial if explained elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement patents must clearly limit claim to the improvement, not entire prior machine
rubrics_metrics.description: The description of an improvement, when an improvement is the real subject-matter, should be made in such a manner as will clearly show that the improvement only is claimed by the patentee; if a machine substantially existed before, the patent should be confined to his improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the effect is the same, the patentee's claim should not encompass the whole pre-existing machine. If the combination in all its parts is entirely new (producing well-known effects), then the whole machine may be claimed as new.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claiming parts of a machine, specify and point them out
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the invention embraces only one or more parts of a machine (e.g., a coulter of a plough), the part or parts claimed must be specified and pointed out so that constructors, other inventors, and the public may know how to make the invention and what is withdrawn from general use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear pointing out prevents overbroad claims that would unduly restrict prior art or the public's use of the rest of the machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater particularity required when claiming both a new ingredient and a combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Where both a new ingredient and a combination of old ingredients embodied in the same machine are claimed, greater particularity is required, since the patentee's property consists not only in the new ingredient but also in the new combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is essential the invention be fully described so its precise nature is known to the public; be explicit about both the ingredient and the claimed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency requirements for a combination of old ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: In a claim for a combination where all ingredients are old and the invention consists entirely in a new combination of old ingredients producing a new and useful result, 'such combination is sufficiently described, if the ingredients of which it is composed are named, their mode of operation given, and the new and useful result to be accomplished pointed out, so that those skilled in the art, and the public, may know the extent and nature of the claim.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe components, how they operate together, and the new useful effect so skilled artisans can understand the claim's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recital of prior use when claiming an improvement is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention be an improvement and be claimed as such, but nothing is said of any previous use of which the proposed use is an improvement, the patent may be construed as a claim of entire and original discovery; hence the necessity for reciting what had formerly been done and describing a different mode as the improvement claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recite prior art or prior modes to show the claim is a narrower improvement rather than a sweeping discovery. Failure to do so can render the patent void or overbroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine patents must explain the principle and several modes of application
rubrics_metrics.description: For any machine, the patentee 'shall fully explain the principle, and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle or character by which it may be distinguished from other inventions; and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention or discovery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'principle' means the peculiar structure and mode of operation. The patentee should state the device he deems best and also all other modes of producing the same effect he intends to claim. Minute instructions for every variation are unnecessary, but indicating what variations are claimed is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must not be mere abstract principles—need practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee may have discovered a principle of science or law of nature, but he cannot patent it by mere statement; he must give it a practical application to some useful purpose and the specification must show the application of the principle to such special purpose by its incorporation with matter to produce a practical result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care must be taken to describe the principle embodied in a particular organization of matter for a purpose; otherwise the claim risks being declared non-patentable as an abstract function or principle.
